name: Preservation rhinoplasty

lead: Preservation rhinoplasty keeps the nose's original bony and cartilaginous bridge and lowers it as a unit, instead of cutting off a dorsal hump. People seek it for a smaller hump or straighter profile while keeping their natural bridge lines.

The chain runs from a lowered hump with the dorsum intact to a smooth, natural-looking bridge and a refined profile. The term was coined by Daniel in 2018, according to a case-series paper. A 2020 review notes renewed interest as an alternative to hump resection, with claims of favourable aesthetic and functional results; evidence consists of retrospective series, a radiological comparison with hump resection, and registered trials.

paras: The surgeon mobilises the osseocartilaginous vault as a single unit and pushes it down or lets it down (push-down and let-down techniques), preserving natural dorsal lines and mucosa. Several classification systems and hybrid approaches have been proposed. The profile change shows as swelling settles.

Reported problems include hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery and technique-specific issues. It carries the general risks of rhinoplasty, including swelling, asymmetry and revision. It is performed by surgeons under anaesthesia.

angle.text: Preservation rhinoplasty lowers a dorsal hump or straightens the profile while keeping the natural bridge lines, so the bridge stays smooth. The surgeon moves the bridge down as one unit rather than cutting it off. Surgeon reports, mostly case series, describe favourable aesthetic results.

lead: Preservation rhinoplasty, also called dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, refers to techniques that address a dorsal hump or the nasal profile by repositioning rather than removing the natural dorsum. A 2020 review notes a rekindled interest in dorsal preservation as an alternative to conventional hump resection, with claims of superior functional and aesthetic results, and describes mobilising the osseocartilaginous vault as a single unit to avoid disrupting natural structure.[1]

A 2018 article titled as a rhinoplasty revolution popularised the term, and a 2020 case series states that the term was coined by Daniel in 2018 and represents a fundamental change in philosophy.[2][3] Later papers proposed classification systems, hybrid structural approaches and guidelines.[4][5][6]
The evidence base consists of retrospective series and comparisons; no large randomised trial is present in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Push-down, let-down, cartilage conversion, hybrid osteoplasty

paras: Push-down and let-down are two main variants; one study used push-down for humps under 4 mm and let-down for larger ones.[7] A practical classification system, guidelines for primary rhinoplasty and a structural hybrid approach have been published, as have techniques converting cartilage to expand indications.[4][5][6][8][8]

A 100-case series with one-year follow-up reported on decision making in preservation rhinoplasty.[3] A study of 520 patients discussed reasons for dorsal hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery and proposed solutions.[7] A radiological study compared the effect on the internal nasal valve of dorsal preservation versus hump resection.[9] A review of current trends summarises the field.[10]

Human data are retrospective: a 153-patient primary series (100 with one-year follow-up), a 520-patient series on hump relapse, and a quantitative radiological comparison with hump resection.[3][7][9] Registered trials include a completed study of nasal valve angle and area (100 patients) and an active trial of hybrid osteoplasty versus osteotomy (200 patients).[11][12]

timeline.event: Term preservation rhinoplasty coined and article on a rhinoplasty revolution published.[2][3]
Review and modification of dorsal preservation techniques; 100-case series reported.[1][3]
Practical classification system and guidelines for dorsum preservation published.[4][5]
